implementation_notes: cats-retry makes the policy a value over an effect: RetryPolicies.limitRetries[IO](5), limitRetriesByCumulativeDelay, exponentialBackoff, capDelay and fullJitter combine into one policy, and the combinators (retryingOnErrors, retryingOnSomeErrors, retryingOnAllErrors) take the effect plus an error handler that receives RetryDetails - retriesSoFar, cumulativeDelay and nextStepIfUnsuccessful (DelayAndRetry(d) or GiveUp) - so logging and metrics are part of the retry rather than bolted on. The wait happens through the effect's Temporal instance (cats-effect IO), so it is a suspended timer rather than a blocked thread, and the whole loop is testable with TestControl's virtual time. Use it in cats-effect stacks where the retry must compose with Resource, Ref and the rest of the effect system; a plain Future.recoverWith loop remains the lightweight alternative.
code_sketch:
val policy = RetryPolicies.exponentialBackoff[IO](100.millis)
  .join(RetryPolicies.limitRetries[IO](5))

val result: IO[String] = retryingOnErrors(flakyRequest)(
  policy = policy,
  errorHandler = ResultHandler.retryOnAllErrors((err, details) =>
    logger.warn(s"${details.retriesSoFar}: $err"))
)
pitfalls: Policies are values and must be built per call site (or shared deliberately): limitRetries without a delay retries immediately, which is the storm pattern.
RetryDetails.nextStepIfUnsuccessful is the only place the next delay is known - logging the delay elsewhere duplicates policy logic and drifts.
The retry runs in the effect's error channel: a defect (an unchecked throwable that cats-effect treats as fatal) is not retried, which is usually desirable but must be understood.
Because the policy is described over an effect, tests must run on a virtual-time runtime (TestControl) or they sleep in real time.

variants.name: ZIO#retry with a composed Schedule policy
variants.implementation_notes: ZIO turns the retry policy into a Schedule value: Schedule.recurs(5) counts attempts, Schedule.exponential(100.millis) produces the growing delay, jittered adds randomness, and the <*, && and || combinators compose them, so retry(policy) on an effect drives the loop; a schedule is a pure, time-aware state machine whose decisions come back as time intervals, which is what makes 'retry with exponential backoff, but give up after a minute' two schedules combined rather than hand-written logic. Because the policy is an ordinary value it can be logged, shared and simulated, and repeat uses the same type for polling loops. Choose it inside a ZIO application; cats-retry is the equivalent for cats-effect.
variants.code_sketch:
val policy: Schedule[Any, Any, Long] = Schedule.recurs(5) <* Schedule.exponential(100.millis).jittered
val call: ZIO[Any, Throwable, String] = ZIO.attempt(client.fetch()).retry(policy)
pitfalls: Schedule combinators compose by intersection and union of intervals: <* keeps the count while taking the delay, but *> or ++ changes which side drives stopping, so a wrong operator silently changes the attempt count.
Schedule.recurs(0) and Schedule.exponential(0.millis) are legal and produce immediate retries; a jittered exponential without a cap can produce very long waits.
The schedule decides only when to try again - classification still has to be expressed by retrying the errors you mean to (retryWhile/retryUntil or a typed error channel).
A schedule is evaluated against wall-clock instants (now is threaded through step), so tests must use TestClock to avoid real delays.
